description: We're building a team that values clear communication, steady progress, and a finished, well-presented result. The goal is to turn an idea into a working project and to learn from each other along the way. If you want to contribute, take ownership of your part, and see a project through to the demo, you'll fit in well.
summary:
One of us learned what love must sound like from Debussy's Arabesque No. 1. But music can carry more than emotion: it can carry data. Is that orange 28 °C or 31 °C? Your eyes can't tell, and the color scale isn't helping. For blind and low-vision people, NASA's maps can be out of reach entirely. So we stopped just looking at the map and started listening to it: Earth Information Jukebox turns NASA imagery into music you can explore by ear.

The app reads each pixel's color back through NASA's own color legend into the real measurement it represents (temperature, sea ice, vegetation, aerosols) and plays it as music while a scan line sweeps the map from west to east. Higher pitch means a higher value, so shades that are hard to tell apart become differences you can hear. Pause, and the arrow keys let you hear any single place.

Listen for the bells: in the air-temperature record, one rings wherever the air reaches 37°C or hotter, so extreme heat becomes something you can count by ear.

Ten NASA records are included, five from the Earth Information Center and five from NASA's GIBS satellite imagery service. Everything works by keyboard and by ear, with a text description of every frame and live narration for screen readers. We state our limits openly, including where the sound is deliberately exaggerated.
details: Our project pairs visual frames from NASA's Earth Information Center with dynamic soundscapes through sonification. Users choose a distinct visualization(as night lights or carbon dioxide concentrations), and depending on our program's analysis of visual attributes(as color spectrums and pixel density) to map them into musical parameters as pitch, tempo, rhythm and instrumentation. There are two modes: orchestra, for deeper emotional appeal, and the scientific mode, which showcases pure data with nothing to distract from analyzing the information. The user is free to highlight only the desired variables(only the red spectrum, for example) by himself, just as conducting an orchestra, where each different information is the artist that can be examined individually, as well as choosing a particular point on a map and hear how it sounds both. This approach enables a deeper understanding of information without any words: drums are enough to show the intensity, and low note on bass is enough to demonstrate that the region is comparably cold. The versatility is the major benefit: the user is able to choose the mode, tempo, key, scale and even control the mood and sound, and each values are relative, normalised across all frames of the record so that change over time stays audible.
